# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–28 (Complete – Updated 199)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Winter of seventh year after Waterloo**. John Sedley deceased (died peacefully in sleep; buried at Brompton churchyard beside wife). Mr. Osborne deceased (died four days after stroke; found at foot of dressing-table). Major Dobbin appointed executor of Osborne's will. Rawdon governs Coventry Island. Georgy established as heir. **Continental tour progressing**: Amelia, Georgy, Jos, and Major Dobbin on steamship and carriage tour; landed Rotterdam, traveled to Cologne, now established in Pumpernickel (a small German principality) for autumn/winter season. **Year noted as 1830 (French Revolution occurred this year)**.
- **Major locations**: London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Gaunt House, Regent Club, Knightsbridge Barracks, Russell Square, Brompton, Conduit Street, Hart Street Bloomsbury, Southampton Row, Kensington Gardens, Camberwell, Slaughters' Inn, Haymarket Theatre, Gillespie Street); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate (deed to pastures discovered to be forged by Madrek Orlwood; Feena Stenworth found work there and did not return); Piccadilly; Madras; St. Helena; Cape; Southampton; Staveton; Belgium (Brussels, Mount St. John, Waterloo, Laeken); Bengal; Salford; Regent's Park; Richmond (Star and Garter); Gulton; Harrowgate; Hill farms; Roehampton; Hampton Court; Calcutta; Jamaica; Rotterdam; Cologne; Free City of Judenstadt; Rhine region; Rhineland; **Pumpernickel** (small German principality with Court, theatre, Duke's schloss, Prime Minister's lodgings, Aurelius Platz, Zwieback's Conditorey, Saint Michael's Fountain, Artillery Place, Stadthaus, Town Hall, Redoute, gardens with Trophonius' cave, nymphbath, Niagara cataract); Mirecombe; Dunholt; Dunwick; Quenwick; Humbourg-Schlippenschloppen; Ems; Aix-la-Chapelle; Baden-Baden; Salwick; Elephant (lodging-house, Room No. 90/92); Boulogne; Dieppe; Portman Square; Brussels; Paris; Wildbad; Strasburg; St. Petersburg; Toplitz; Vienna; Pincian Hill (Rome); Naples; Castle Gaunt; Trinity House; White Friars; Chiswick; University of Schoppenhausen; Leipzig; Dresden; Schoppenhausen; Clapham.

## Rebecca at Pumpernickel (Chapter 27–28)

**Arrival and Gaming Encounters**: At Stadthaus gaming, Jos remained at play-table. Woman in foreign accent revealed herself as **Rebecca (Madame de Raudon)**, formerly involved with Rawdon Crawley. Spoke of seeing "dear Amelia," noted she "looked pretty and happy."

**Seduction of Jos (Chapter 28)**: Rebecca in pink domino (faded, soiled) led Jos into garret at Elephant lodging-house (Room No. 92). Hid evidence of degradation (rouge-pot, brandy bottle, plate of broken meat), smoothed hair. Gave tender looks, claimed heart first learned to beat at Jos's presence; denied giving George encouragement; asserted marital duties paramount; promised preserve virtue "to her dying day, or until...Colonel Crawley's...cruelty had rendered odious." Jos departed convinced "that she was the most virtuous, as she was one of the most fascinating of women" and resolved she must quit that place, take quiet lodging, and that Amelia must befriend her.

**Becky's True Nature**: After Jos departed, "Becky bowed Jos out of her little garret with as much grace as if it was a palace of which she did the honours." Max and Fritz (students from Schoppenhausen) came out of hole, pipe in mouth. She mimicked Jos while munching cold bread and sausage and drinking brandy-and-water. **Becky liked the life**: "She was at home with everybody in the place, pedlars, punters, tumblers, students and all. She was of a wild, roving nature, inherited from father and mother, who were both Bohemians, by taste and circumstance." Students reported: Becky advertised concert at Leipzig that did not occur (claimed pianist fell ill at Dresden). She won money at trente-et-quarante using young Georgy to play for her; planned to spend money on wine, theatre, or Cognac in Aurelius Garden rather than buy her own concert tickets.

## Jos and Dobbin Consult; Major Dobbin's Response (Chapter 28)

Jos walked to Dobbin's lodgings with great solemnity and imparted affecting history without mentioning gaming. Two gentlemen consulted as to best means of being useful to Mrs. Becky.

**Major's Distrust**: When Major heard from Jos, excitement was "quite the reverse from a pleasurable one"; he called her "The little minx." Never had slightest liking for her; heartily mistrusted her from first moment when "her green eyes had looked at, and turned away from, his own." Said: "That little devil brings mischief wherever she goes." Questioned who knows what sort of life she has been leading, why abroad and alone, why left husband. Recalled Rawdon was "confounded blackleg" who cheated poor George. Remembered scandal about separation. Jos tried in vain to convince Dobbin that Mrs. Becky was "in all respects a most injured and virtuous female."

**Appeal to Amelia (Chapter 28)**: Major insisted: "By Gad, sir, she's the finest lady I ever met in my life. I say at once, let us go and ask her if this woman ought to be visited or not." Major thought: "I am sure of my case. Emmy...was at one time cruelly and deservedly jealous of Rebecca, never mentioned her name but with a shrinking and terror--a jealous woman never forgives." Pair crossed street to Mrs. George's house, where she was warbling at music lesson with Madame Strumpff.

## Amelia's Response to Rebecca (Chapter 28)

Jos opened business with usual pomp. Becky had no friend in world; her story affected him greatly; family most cruel; she tried to kill herself (carried laudanum); lived in miserable little room at Elephant, roof top.

**Becky Prepares and Visits**: Becky saw them from garret and had time to dismiss Max and Fritz before landlord led them upstairs (landlord knew Mrs. Osborne great favourite at Court, respected her accordingly). Payne, staid English maid and personal attendant upon Amelia, would be displaced to give Becky her room.

**Amelia's Sympathy and Becky's False History**: Amelia's frankness and kindness touched Becky. She returned Emmy's caresses with "something very like gratitude, and an emotion which, if it was not lasting, for a moment was almost genuine." Becky's lucky stroke was claiming child "torn from her arms shrieking." Amelia cried out: "Oh, Rebecca, my poor dear suffering friend, I know what it is to lose a boy...But please Heaven yours will be restored to you, as a merciful merciful Providence has brought me back mine."

**Becky's Lies Multiply and Full False History (Chapter 28)**: Becky owned to agonies regarding child, "not perhaps without a twinge of conscience. It jarred upon her to be obliged to commence instantly to tell lies in reply to so much confidence and simplicity. But that is the misfortune of beginning with this kind of forgery. When one fib becomes due as it were, you must forge another to take up the old acceptance; and so the stock of your lies in circulation inevitably multiplies, and the danger of detection increases every day." Two women talked an hour or more. Becky gave full version: marriage with Rawdon viewed by family with utmost hostility; sister-in-law (artful woman) poisoned husband's mind against her; he formed odious connections, estranged affections; she bore everything—poverty, neglect, coldness "for the sake of her child"; finally driven to demand separation when wretch asked she sacrifice fair fame for advancement through Marquis of Steyne—"The atrocious monster!" Forced to flee husband's roof by insult, coward pursued revenge by taking child from her. Thus Becky claimed she was "a wanderer, poor, unprotected, friendless, and wretched."

**Amelia's Indignation and Offer of Hospitality (Chapter 28)**: Emmy received story with indignation at conduct of "miserable Rawdon" and "unprincipled Steyne." Eyes made notes of admiration for every sentence describing persecutions and husband's falling away. During separation scene recitation, Emmy "retired altogether behind her pocket-handkerchief, so that the consummate little tragedian must have been charmed to see the effect which her performance produced on her audience." Later, Emmy offered: "She may have Payne's room, who can go upstairs...The poor creature, after all her sufferings...the poor dear thing! quite alone and absolutely forced to give lessons in singing to get her bread--and not have her here!"

**Dobbin's Continued Opposition (Chapter 28)**: Major, seeing great crisis had come, nevertheless continued to implore Sedley in most energetic terms to beware of Rebecca; eagerly, almost frantically, adjured Jos not to receive her. Besought him to inquire regarding her; told how heard she was in company of gamblers and people of ill repute; pointed out what evil she had done in former days, how she and Crawley misled poor George into ruin, how she was now parted from her husband, perhaps for good reason. William implored Jos "with all the eloquence which he could bring to bear, and a great deal more energy than this quiet gentleman was ordinarily in the habit of showing, to keep Rebecca out of his household."

**Major's Allusion to Emmy's Past Jealousy**: When Major said, "She was not always your friend, Amelia," Emmy looked him "almost fiercely in the face, said, 'For shame, Major Dobbin!' and after having fired this shot, she walked out of the room with a most majestic air and shut her own door briskly on herself and her outraged dignity." Behind closed door, Emmy declared: "To allude to THAT!...Oh, it was cruel of him to remind me of it." She gazed at George's picture hanging on wall with portrait of boy underneath. "It was cruel of him. If I had forgiven it, ought he to have spoken? No. And it is from his own lips that I know how wicked and groundless my jealousy was; and that you were pure--oh, yes, you were pure, my saint in heaven!"

**Major Dobbin's Despair (Chapter 28)**: Major's allusion "undone the work of many a year--the long laborious edifice of a life of love and constancy--raised too upon what secret and hidden foundations, wherein lay buried passions, uncounted struggles, unknown sacrifices--a little word was spoken, and down fell the fair palace of hope--one word, and away flew the bird which he had been trying all his life to lure!"

## Key Character States
- **Amelia**: Believes Becky's story; has forgiven past jealousy regarding George; committed to befriending Becky; offended by Dobbin's allusion to that jealousy; still devoted to George's memory.
- **Major Dobbin**: Deeply distrusts Becky; despairs over Amelia's sympathy toward her; has spent life loving Amelia secretly; ruined work of years by one allusion to her past jealousy of Becky.
- **Jos Sedley**: Convinced of Becky's virtue and misery; planning to help her settle respectably.
- **Rebecca**: In Pumpernickel living vagabond existence; manipulative; using Jos's gullibility; gambles actively; liars multiply upon her; lacks genuine remorse.
- **Rawdon Crawley**: Separated permanently from Rebecca; financially settled on three hundred pounds per year with understanding she never trouble him again; transformed morally; governs Coventry Island.
